title: Where Could I Go?
hook: a sage's last days, and the poem's last word on freedom
carry: mukti isn't a finish line; the self is already free
tomorrow: a brass lamp in a suitcase. can worship travel?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy lay still in Madurai: atman isn't the body; dive for its source. Today, the poem's last word, and the end of this year's lineage track.

April 1950, at the foot of Arunachala. Ramana is seventy and very ill; a cancer on his arm has come back after surgery. Every evening, people file past the door of his little room to see him. Many are crying. They keep saying it: Bhagavan is leaving us. And he answers, in the words his devotees remember, roughly: they say I'm going away. But where could I go? I am here.
screen: `APRIL 1950: THE SAGE IS DYING.` → `THEY SAY: HE'S LEAVING US.` → `WHERE COULD I GO? I AM HERE.`

segments.voice: His devotees didn't hear that as bravery about dying. They heard what his whole life had said: the self was never the body, so it has nowhere to go. It's the teaching his Forty Verses close on. Hindus call the goal of the spiritual life mukti, or moksha: freedom, release. It's easy to picture it as a finish line, reached after years. Ramana's last verses say no. First he brings back an old friend. Some say: two while practicing, one only at the end. Not so, he says, in paraphrase: searching or found, who is the tenth man but oneself? That's the Panchadashi's counter, who counted nine and wept, and was the tenth the whole time. He wasn't less the tenth before he noticed. Next: the thought I am bound, and the thought I will be free, last only as long as the one who thinks I am bound lasts. Ask who is bound, and what's left is the self, always free. Then the last verse. People debate what liberation looks like: with form, without form, or both. In paraphrase: the ending of the ego that asks which kind it'll be, that is liberation. So the poem closes the way his life did, by sending the question back. Not where am I going, but who is going. This track has walked through Shankara's commentary on the sutras, the Panchadashi's pictures and Ramana's Tamil lines. Different teachers, one steady turn toward the one who reads.
screen: `THE SELF HAS NOWHERE TO GO.` · `MUKTI: NOT A FINISH LINE.` · `SEARCHING OR FOUND: THE TENTH MAN.` · `ASK WHO IS BOUND.` · then, large: `WHO IS GOING?`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for about a minute, around the room or down a hall, with nowhere to get to. Let each step be the whole trip. Then sit for the rest of the time, and if a thought comes measuring progress, ask gently who wants to get there.
Ramana's Forty Verses: a Tamil poem on what is, that ends by asking who wants to be free.
The line to take with you: mukti isn't a finish line; the self is already free. The lineage track, complete.

howItsDone: Ramana's followers read the closing verses as the poem's summary and return to the question 'who am I?' rather than measuring progress; pilgrims still visit his shrine at the foot of Arunachala.

chat.meaning: Ramana's verse: searching or found, the tenth man is oneself. Mukti isn't a place reached later; ask who is going.

tie.story: The Panchadashi's counter wept for a missing tenth man, and Ramana's verse says that, searching or found, the counter was the tenth all along.
tie.friend: Priya doesn't have to wait for a 'ready' moment; what she's looking for is the one already doing the looking.
tie.you: what are you waiting to finally feel?
